options(scipen = 999)

## Recap

Last week we learned about **simple linear regression**

$$y_i = b_0 +b_1x_{1i} + \epsilon_i$$

While our models sometimes generally captured the trend, there still was a good amount of prediction error. 

Maybe we can create a better predictive model by using more than one explanatory variable (aka **predictor**)!


##

**Simple** linear regression = only one $X$

$$y_i = b_0 +b_1x_{1i} + \epsilon_i$$

**Multiple** linear regression = multiple $X$'s

$$y_i = b_0 +b_1x_{1i} + b_2 x_{2i} + ... + b_p x_{pi} \epsilon_i$$

# Ex: Penguins model

In your homework you looked at the `penguins` data.

Let's see if we can build a good predictive model for a penguin's bill depth ($Y$).

## Model 1

We will start by using a penguin's flipper length as a predictor ($X$) for it's bill depth ($Y$).

<center>

| Variable | Symbol | Relationship | Type |
|---|-------------|-----------------|---------|
| Bill depth | $y$ | Response | Numeric |
| Flipper length | $x_1$ | Predictor | Numeric |

</center>

## Model 1 Visually

```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(
  penguins, 
  aes(
    x = flipper_len, 
    y = bill_dep
  )
) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", 
    se = FALSE
  )
```

## Estimating Model 1

```{r}
#| out-width: 40%
#| echo: false
ggplot(
  penguins, 
  aes(
    x = flipper_len, 
    y = bill_dep
  )
) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", 
    se = FALSE
  )
```

. . .

```{r}
penguins_model_1 <- lm(bill_dep ~ flipper_len, data = penguins)
tidy(penguins_model_1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
model_1_b0 <- round(penguins_model_1$coefficients[1], digits)
model_1_b1 <- round(penguins_model_1$coefficients[2], digits)
```


**Predicted Bill Depth = `r model_1_b0` + `r model_1_b1` $\times$ Flipper Length**

## Assessing fit of Model 1

Estimated Model 1:

**Predicted Bill Depth = `r model_1_b0` + `r model_1_b1` $\times$ Flipper Length**

. . .

*Is this line a good fit for the data?*

. . .

Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) can help us asses!

```{r}
rmse(penguins_model_1, data = penguins)
```

The predictions from Model 1 are off by roughly `r round(rmse(penguins_model_1, data = penguins)
, 2)` mm, on average.

. . .

Our data only have bill depths between 13 mm and 21.5 mm, so this model is not doing a great job...

## Model 2

Let's also consider using both body mass and flipper length!

<center>

| Variable | Symbol | Relationship | Type |
|---|-------------|-----------------|---------|
| Bill depth | $y$ | Response | Numeric |
| Flipper length | $x_1$ | Predictor | Numeric |
| Body mass | $x_2$ | Predictor | Numeric |

</center>


## Model 2 Visually

It gets harder/impossible to visualize our model the more predictors we have. Instead we can still look at a plot of $Y$ and one $X$ at a time to see if we think they are linearly related.


```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(
  penguins, 
  aes(
    x = body_mass, 
    y = bill_dep
  )
) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(
    method = "lm", 
    se = FALSE
  )
```

## Fitting Model 2

```{r}
penguins_model_2 <- lm(bill_dep ~ flipper_len + body_mass, data = penguins)
tidy(penguins_model_2)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
model_2_b0 <- round(penguins_model_2$coefficients[1], 1)
model_2_b1 <- round(penguins_model_2$coefficients[2], 1)
model_2_b2 <- round(penguins_model_2$coefficients[3], 4)
```


**Predicted Bill Depth = `r model_2_b0` + `r model_2_b1` $\times$ Flipper Length**  
**+ `r model_2_b2` $\times$ Body Mass**

## Assessing Model 2 fit

Estimated Model 2:

**Predicted Bill Depth = `r model_2_b0` + `r model_2_b1` $\times$ Flipper Length**  
**+ `r model_2_b2` $\times$ Body Mass**

. . .

*Is this line a good fit for the data?*

. . .

```{r}
rmse(penguins_model_2, data = penguins)
```

. . . 

Hmmmm, not much better.

## Examining the data

```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(
  penguins, 
  aes(
    x = flipper_len, 
    y = bill_dep
  )
) + 
  geom_point()
```

*What is causing this split in the data??*

## Accounting for species

```{r}
#| output-location: column
ggplot(
  penguins, 
  aes(
    x = flipper_len, 
    y = bill_dep,
    color = species
  )
) + 
  geom_point()
```

Now we see a much different (positive) trend!

## Model 3

Let's using flipper length and species to predict flipper length!

<center>

| Variable | Symbol | Relationship | Type |
|---|-------------|-----------------|---------|
| Bill depth | $y$ | Response | Numeric |
| Flipper length | $x_1$ | Predictor | Numeric |
| Species | $x_2$ | Predictor | Categorical |

</center>


## Model 3 visually

```{r}
#| output-location: column
library(moderndive)
ggplot(
  penguins, 
  aes(
    x = flipper_len, 
    y = bill_dep,
    color = species
  )
) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_parallel_slopes(se = FALSE)
```

We use the `geom_parallel_slopes()` function from the moderndive R package. (`geom_smooth()` would do different behavior we won't go into in this class!)

## Estimating Model 3

```{r}
penguins_model_3 <- lm(bill_dep ~ flipper_len + species, data = penguins)
tidy(penguins_model_3)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
model_3_b0 <- round(
  penguins_model_3$coefficients[1], 
  digits = digits
  )
model_3_b1 <- round(
  penguins_model_3$coefficients["flipper_len"], 
  digits = digits
  )
model_3_b2 <- round(
  penguins_model_3$coefficients["speciesChinstrap"], 
  digits = digits
  )
model_3_b3 <- round(
  penguins_model_3$coefficients["speciesGentoo"], 
  digits = digits
  )
```


Predicted Bill Depth = `r model_3_b0` + `r model_3_b1` $\times$  Flipper Length  
\+ `r model_3_b2` $\times$ I(Species = Chinstrap)  
\+ `r model_3_b3` $\times$ I(Species = Gentoo)

## Assessing Model 3 fit

Estimated Model 3:

**Predicted Bill Depth = `r model_3_b0` + `r model_3_b1` $\times$  Flipper Length**  
**\+ `r model_3_b2` $\times$ I(Species = Chinstrap)**  
**\+ `r model_3_b3` $\times$ I(Species = Gentoo)**

```{r}
rmse(penguins_model_3, data = penguins)
```

. . . 

| Model | Predictors | RMSE |
|:----|:-----------------|:----|
| 1 | Flipper Length | `r round(rmse(penguins_model_1, data = penguins), 2)` |
| 2 | Flipper Length & Body Mass| `r round(rmse(penguins_model_2, data = penguins), 2)` |
| 3 | Flipper Length & Species | `r round(rmse(penguins_model_3, data = penguins), 2)` |


## Examining Model 3

Estimated Model 3:

**Predicted Bill Depth = `r model_3_b0` + `r model_3_b1` $\times$  Flipper Length**  
**\+ `r model_3_b2` $\times$ I(Species = Chinstrap)**  
**\+ `r model_3_b3` $\times$ I(Species = Gentoo)**

. . .

- *What are those I() functions?*
- *What about the Adelie penguins?*

# Categorical predictors

## Indicator functions

**I(Species = Chinstrap)**  and **I(Species = Gentoo)**

The I() function is

- Called an **indicator function**
- 1 if true, and 0 if false
- Used for categorical predictors (since we can't do math with categorical variables)

## Categorical Predictors ($X$'s)

**Predicted Bill Depth = `r model_3_b0` + `r model_3_b1` $\times$ Flipper Length**  
**\+ `r model_3_b2` $\times$ I(Species = Chinstrap)**  
**\+ `r model_3_b3` $\times$ I(Species = Gentoo)**

- Recall there are three levels for species, but notice only 2 species levels appear in our model 
- **Reference level** is the omitted level for a categorical variable 
- For every categorical variable with $k$ levels, there will be $k-1$ predictors in the model (because of math...)

##

**Predicted Bill Depth = `r model_3_b0` + `r model_3_b1` $\times$ Flipper Length**  
**\+ `r model_3_b2` $\times$ I(Species = Chinstrap)**  
**\+ `r model_3_b3` $\times$ I(Species = Gentoo)**

Predicted Bill Depth for a Gentoo penguin with a flipper length of 200mm:

```{r}
#| echo: false

pred_1 <- model_3_b0 + model_3_b1 * 200 + model_3_b2 * 0 + model_3_b3 * 1
```


`r model_3_b0` + `r model_3_b1` $\times$ 200 + `r model_3_b2` $\times$ 0 + `r model_3_b3` $\times$ 1 = `r round(pred_1, digits = 1)` mm

. . .

Predicted Bill Depth for a Chinstrap penguin with a flipper length of 200mm:

```{r}
#| echo: false

pred_2 <- model_3_b0 + model_3_b1 * 200 + model_3_b2 * 1 + model_3_b3 * 0
```

`r model_3_b0` + `r model_3_b1` $\times$ 200 + `r model_3_b2` $\times$ 1 + `r model_3_b3` $\times$ 0 = `r round(pred_2, digits = 1)` mm

. . .

Predicted Bill Depth for an Adelie penguin with a flipper length of 200mm:

```{r}
#| echo: false

pred_3 <- model_3_b0 + model_3_b1 * 200 + model_3_b2 * 0 + model_3_b3 * 0
```

`r model_3_b0` + `r model_3_b1` $\times$ 200 + `r model_3_b2` $\times$ 0 + `r model_3_b3` $\times$ 0 = `r round(pred_3, digits = 1)` mm

## Invidiual versus shared model

*Why don't we just split the data set up by species and fit a line for each?*

By using a single model for all of our data:

- we pool information across the different species. This can lead to lower error (more precise prediction)
- allows for shared slope, different y-intercepts

## Model 4

Now let's use flipper length, species, and body mass in our model!

<center>

| Variable | Symbol | Relationship | Type |
|---|-------------|-----------------|---------|
| Bill depth | $y$ | Response | Numeric |
| Flipper length | $x_1$ | Predictor | Numeric |
| Species | $x_2$ | Predictor | Categorical |
| Body mass | $x_3$ | Predictor | Numeric |

</center>


## Estimating Model 4

```{r}
penguins_model_4 <- lm(bill_dep ~ flipper_len + species + body_mass, data = penguins)
tidy(penguins_model_4)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
model_4_b0 <- round(
  penguins_model_4$coefficients[1], 
  digits = digits
  )
model_4_b1 <- round(
  penguins_model_4$coefficients["flipper_len"], 
  digits = 2
  )
model_4_b2 <- round(
  penguins_model_4$coefficients["speciesChinstrap"], 
  digits = digits
  )
model_4_b3 <- round(
  penguins_model_4$coefficients["speciesGentoo"], 
  digits = digits
  )
model_4_b4 <- round(
  penguins_model_4$coefficients["body_mass"], 
  digits = 4
  )
```

Predicted Bill Depth = `r model_4_b0` + `r model_4_b1` $\times$ Flipper Length  
\+ `r model_4_b2` $\times$ I(Species = Chinstrap)  
\+ `r model_4_b3` $\times$ I(Species = Gentoo)  
\+ `r model_4_b4` $\times$ Body Mass

## Assessing Model 4 fit

Estimated Model 4:

**Predicted Bill Depth = `r model_4_b0` + `r model_4_b1` $\times$ Flipper Length**  
**\+ `r model_4_b2` $\times$ I(Species = Chinstrap)**  
**\+ `r model_4_b3` $\times$ I(Species = Gentoo)**  
**\+ `r model_4_b4` $\times$ Body Mass**

. . .

```{r}
rmse(penguins_model_4, data = penguins)
```

## Comparing Models

| Model | Predictors | RMSE |
|:----|:-----------------|:----|
| 1 | Flipper Length | `r round(rmse(penguins_model_1, data = penguins), 2)` |
| 2 | Flipper Length & Body Mass| `r round(rmse(penguins_model_2, data = penguins), 2)` |
| 3 | Flipper Length & Species | `r round(rmse(penguins_model_3, data = penguins), 2)` |
| 4 | Flipper Length & Species & Body Mass | `r round(rmse(penguins_model_4, data = penguins), 2)` |

. . .

We used RMSE to compare models, there are other commonly used metrics!

# Model Evaluation

## Common evaluation metrics

- $R^2$
- Adjusted $R^2$
- Root Mean Square Error (RMSE)


## $R^2$

$R^2$ is the proportion of variation in $Y$ explained by model.

- Informs about how well the model fits the data
- Bounded between 0 and 1
- Should only be used to compare models with the same number of predictors!!

## $R^2$

```{r}
glance(penguins_model_1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
model_1_eval <- glance(penguins_model_1)
```

Model 1 explains `r 100 * round(model_1_eval$r.squared, 2)`% of the variation in Bill Depth.

## Adjusted $R^2$

A major issue with $R^2$ is that it will always increase when you add another predictor $X$, even if it is not a better model.

A more responsible metric to use is Adjusted $R^2$, which penalizes having more predictors in your model.

## Adjusted $R^2$

When comparing models with multiple predictors we rely on Adjusted $R^2$


```{r}
glance(penguins_model_1)
glance(penguins_model_2)
```


## Root Mean Square Error

$RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{(y_1-\hat y_1)^2 + (y_2-\hat y_2)^2 + ... + (y_n-\hat y_n)^2}{n}}$

- "Essentially" measuring average prediction error for our model
- Lowest possible value is 0
- Same units as $Y$

##

```{r}
rmse(penguins_model_1, data = penguins)
```

The predictions from model 1 are, on average, off by `r round(rmse(penguins_model_1, data = penguins), 2)` mm. 

```{r}
rmse(penguins_model_4, data = penguins)
```

The predictions from model 4 are, on average, off by `r round(rmse(penguins_model_4, data = penguins), 2)` mm. 


# Overfitting

Can we keep adding all the variables and try to get an EXCELLENT model fit?

## Overfitting

- We are fitting the model to sample data.

- Our goal is to build a model that will predict well on on other data (with unknown $Y$).

- If we make our model too perfect for our sample data, the model may not perform as well with other data.

- In this case we would be overfitting the data.

- We can use **model validation** techniques.

## Splitting the data

To avoid overfitting we can split our data

- Some of the data will be reserved for estimating our model (called **training** your model)
- The rest of the data will be reserved for evaluating the prediction of our model (called **testing** your model)

## Splitting the data (Train vs. Test)

Load the rsample and modelr packages and set a seed.
```{r}
library(rsample)
library(modelr)
set.seed(8236)
```

Let's use 75% of our sample data to train, then the other 25% to test our model.
```{r}
penguins_split <- initial_split(penguins, prop = 0.75) # 75% to 25% split
penguins_train_data <- training(penguins_split)
penguins_test_data <- testing(penguins_split)
```

. . .
 
```{r}
nrow(penguins)
nrow(penguins_train_data)
nrow(penguins_test_data)
```


## Training Model 4

Fit the model with the training data
```{r}
model_4_train <- lm(
  bill_dep ~ flipper_len + species + body_mass,  
  data = penguins_train_data
)
```


## Testing Model 4

In-sample (train) RMSE
```{r}
rmse(
  model_4_train, 
  data = penguins_train_data
)
```

Out-of-sample (test) RMSE
```{r}
rmse(
  model_4_train, 
  data = penguins_test_data
)
```

## Comparing out-of-sample RMSE

```{r}
#| echo: false

model_1_train <- lm(
  bill_dep ~ flipper_len,  
  data = penguins_train_data
)
model_2_train <- lm(
  bill_dep ~ flipper_len + body_mass,  
  data = penguins_train_data
)
model_3_train <- lm(
  bill_dep ~ flipper_len + species,  
  data = penguins_train_data
)

rmse_df <- data.frame(
  model = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
  in_rmse = c(
    rmse(
      model_1_train, 
      data = penguins_train_data
    ),
    rmse(
      model_2_train, 
      data = penguins_train_data
    ),
    rmse(
      model_3_train, 
      data = penguins_train_data
    ),
    rmse(
      model_4_train, 
      data = penguins_train_data
    )
  ),
  out_rmse = c(
    rmse(
      model_1_train, 
      data = penguins_test_data
    ),
    rmse(
      model_2_train, 
      data = penguins_test_data
    ),
    rmse(
      model_3_train, 
      data = penguins_test_data
    ),
    rmse(
      model_4_train, 
      data = penguins_test_data
    )
  )
) |> 
  mutate(out_rmse = round(out_rmse, 3))
```


| Model | Predictors | Out-of-sample RMSE |
|:--|:-----------------|:----|
| 1 | Flipper Length | `r rmse_df[1, 3]` |
| 2 | Flipper Length & Body Mass| `r rmse_df[2, 3]` |
| 3 | Flipper Length & Species | `r rmse_df[3, 3]` |
| 4 | Flipper Length & Species & Body Mass | `r rmse_df[4, 3]` |
